newsitem.title: USA: America Online to unveil the "new" AOL.
newsitem.headline: America Online to unveil the "new" AOL.

text.p: The stock of America Online Inc. will begin trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Monday amid great fanfare with a block party on Broad Street and the company's launch of what it is calling the "new AOL."

Steve Case, the chairman and CEO of America Online, will ring the opening bell at the NYSE as part of the day-long hoopla, and then will hold a conference call with other top AOL executives and reporters.
Case is expected to discuss how AOL is reinventing itself, amid a turbulent time in the online services arena and at AOL.

While AOL is still the largest commercial online service in the world, with 6.2 million subscribers, the company has been undergoing many pressures in recent months, most memorably its almost 19-hour service outage in August.

The online service is also seeing pressure from the Internet, as some members leave for direct Internet access, and from the rapid innovation on the Net, its new president quit abruptly in June and members are joining at slower rates.
"They have taken a lot of hits lately," said Emily Green, an analyst at Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass.
"They have had a need to buff up their image and to make sure people are aware that they want to stay out ahead of the competition," Green added.
Case will talk about a new business model for the online giant, with a key focus of the strategy its new version of its service software, Version 3.0, launched this summer.
He will also discuss some new revenue generating areas, analysts said.

One big focus for Case is to keep the churn rate at bay, analysts said, referring to the rate at which customers who join briefly and then leave the service. AOL is starting several programmes to help keep its members from leaving.
Instead of inundating the world with floppy disks of its software, AOL will be sending out video tapes to new members, to help them learn everything they can about America Online.

"Steve is convinced that if he can spend one hour in a member's living room ... that will be a key way to reduce churn," said Peter Krasilovsky, an analyst with Arlen Communications Inc. in Bethesda, Md. "So he will send out a video tape which will show people what they can do with AOL."
The new version of AOL has 22 categories, or areas, almost double the prior version. AOL will also begin sending electronic mail to members with tips on using the service.

The company also plans a new advertising campaign in October, during prime-time television, to replace its current campaign that runs usually during late-night television, with ads that some analysts described as "weird" or "awful."

"It's going to cost them a lot," said Abhishek Gami, an analyst with Nesbitt Burns Securities in Chicago. "They will spend $500 million to $525 million in cash and marketing expenses for the year," Gami estimated.
Analysts said Case will also talk about several new revenue sources for AOL beyond its subscription revenues, such as advertising, transactions and a focus on corporate users.

The Dulles, Va.,-based company will likely tout some new corporate installations of AOL, where companies like Century 21, and the New York Stock Exchange, are using private "label" versions of AOL for their own corporate "intranets."

"They figured that a lot of things that people use Lotus Notes and intranets for they can provide," said Forrester's Green, adding that an organisation with a private AOL can get member names, bulletin boards, chat, content areas, etc.
AOL will announce the NYSE as a new corporate user Monday.
Analysts said these moves are necessary if AOL is to reach Case's goal of 10 million members by next year.
